summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Frame Relay service. It does not specify a standard for the Internet community. It was replaced by RFC 1604.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of gauges for watching how a frame relay connection is doing. A later document replaced it.

questions: how to monitor frame relay service
subtitle: Standard monitoring objects for Frame Relay network services.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay service providers and customers needed a standard way to monitor and manage Frame Relay connections, but no agreed-upon set of managed objects existed for this purpose.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends the SNMP MIB (Management Information Base) with specialized managed objects for Frame Relay services, organized into groups for logical ports, VC signaling, PVC endpoints, connections, and accounting.
tldr.outcome: Customers can now monitor Frame Relay performance and faults through SNMP, and service providers can offer consistent network management interfaces. This was replaced by RFC 1604, which revised and consolidated the definitions.

today: RFC 1596 is a Standards Track protocol that was replaced by RFC 1604, which revised the definitions based on implementation experience. The SNMPv2-based MIB approach it pioneered remains the standard for monitoring Frame Relay services.

sections.title: Frame Relay Service and Network Management
sections.content:
Frame Relay is a data communications service that uses virtual connections to deliver traffic across networks. Service providers need to monitor these connections for performance and faults, and customers need visibility into their service. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) provides the standard infrastructure for network management, but Frame Relay required specialized managed objects tailored to how Frame Relay services work.

This RFC defines those objects using the SNMPv2 framework. The objects support Customer Network Management (CNM), where a customer's network management station monitors its Frame Relay connections and faults through an SNMP proxy agent provided by the service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame relay is a way to send data through networks using virtual connections. This document defines how to measure and manage those connections using standard network monitoring tools.

sections.title: MIB Architecture and Scope
sections.content:
The MIB objects sit atop MIB II (the standard Internet management objects) and the interface table. The Frame Relay Service MIB manages the Frame Relay portion of the network, not user equipment (which uses the Frame Relay DTE MIB, RFC 1315).

Frame Relay connections come in two types: Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs), which have fixed endpoints and capabilities set at subscription time, and Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs), which are established on demand. This RFC focuses on PVCs.

The service model uses UNI (User-to-Network Interface) and NNI (Network-to-Network Interface) logical ports as the managed endpoints. Customers access the MIB through an SNMP proxy agent within the service provider's network. The MIB models PVC segments through one Frame Relay network; customers with PVCs crossing multiple networks must query separate proxy agents for a complete end-to-end view.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB fits on top of standard network management. It tracks the connections between customer sites and the network, and lets customers see how their virtual circuits are doing.

sections.title: Managed Object Groups
sections.content:
The RFC defines several groups of managed objects. The Frame Relay Service Logical Port Group provides information about the physical and logical interfaces (UNI/NNI ports) on which Frame Relay operates, including addressing schemes, interface type, and VC signaling protocol in use.

The Frame Relay Management VC Signaling Group tracks signaling parameters and errors for the local in-channel signaling protocol that manages virtual circuits. It includes counters for link reliability errors, protocol errors, and channel inactivity events.

The PVC End-Point Group models individual PVC endpoints at each logical port. Each endpoint is identified by a DLCI (Data Link Connection Identifier) and contains traffic parameters like Committed Information Rate (CIR), Committed Burst Size (Bc), and Excess Burst Size (Be), along with statistics on frames and octets transmitted and received.

The Frame Relay PVC Connection Group connects PVC endpoints together to model complete virtual circuits. This group handles the creation, modification and deletion of PVCs through SNMP (where the service provider supports such operations).

The Frame Relay Accounting Group tracks resource usage for billing and performance analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are organized into groups: one for the port connections, one for signaling, one for each PVC endpoint's traffic parameters, one for connecting endpoints into complete circuits, and one for tracking usage for billing.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring and Fault Detection
sections.content:
The MIB objects enable customers to retrieve performance data and receive TRAP notifications (alerts) about Frame Relay service events. Customers can monitor the health of their logical ports, observe the PVC signaling protocol's behavior, and track packet and octet counts through their virtual circuits.

The managed objects provide both configuration data (traffic parameters) and operational data (counters, errors). By polling these objects periodically and analyzing trends, a customer's network management system can detect congestion, count delivered frames, identify protocol errors, and monitor compliance with service levels defined in the subscription agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Using these objects, a manager can watch how much traffic is flowing, count errors, see if the connection is stable, and get alerts when something goes wrong.
